# Fourier Analysis {#sec-fourier_analysis}

## Introduction

We need a more precise language to talk about the effect of linear
filters, and the different image components, than to say "sharp" and
"blurry" parts of the image. The Fourier transform provides that
precision. By analogy with temporal frequencies, which describe how
quickly signals vary over time, a **spatial frequency** describes how
quickly a signal varies over space. The Fourier transform lets us
describe a signal as a sum of complex exponentials, each of a different
spatial frequency.

Fourier transforms are the basis of a number of computer vision
approaches and are an important tool to understand images and how linear
spatially invariant filters transform images. There are also important
to understand modern representations such as positional encoding
popularized by transformers @vaswani2017attention.

## Image Transforms

Sometimes it is useful to transform the image pixels into another
representation that might reveal image properties that can be useful for
solving vision tasks. Before we saw that linear filtering is a useful
way of transforming an image. Linear image transforms with the form
$\mathbf{x} =  \mathbf{H} \boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ can be thought
of as a way of changing the initial pixels representation of
$\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}$ into a different representation in
$\mathbf{x}$.

:::{.column-margin}
We use $\mathbf{x}$ to denote an intermediate representation. The representation might not be an image.
:::

This representation is specially interesting when it can
be inverted so that the original pixels can be recovered as
$\boldsymbol\ell_{\texttt{in}}=  \mathbf{H}^{-1} \mathbf{x}$. The
Fourier transform is one of those representations. A useful
representation $\mathbf{x}$ should have a number of interesting

Real part projection curve: a continuous red cosine wave plotted entirely in the R-n plane

Projection lines: thin, translucent grey dashed lines connecting each 3D sphere to its corresponding projection points on the R-n and I-n planes

interactions.label: Frequency (ω)
interactions.teaches: Adjusting the frequency changes how tightly the helix winds around the time axis, corresponding to a higher spatial or temporal frequency.

interactions.label: Damping (σ)

interactions.label: Orbit View

demo_steps.title: The 3D Helical Signal
demo_steps.narration: Welcome to the 3D world of complex exponentials. This black helical curve of discrete points represents the signal z[n] = e^(j ω n). The axial direction represents index n, while the transverse directions represent the Real and Imaginary parts.

demo_steps.title: The Real Component (Cosine)
demo_steps.narration: Let's align our perspective to look straight down the Imaginary axis. The 3D helix collapses into a 2D plane, revealing that the Real part (shown in red) is a pure cosine wave.

demo_steps.title: The Imaginary Component (Sine)
demo_steps.narration: Rotating to look down the Real axis, we see only the Imaginary component (shown in green). It forms a pure sine wave, phase-shifted by 90 degrees relative to the Real part.

demo_steps.title: The Complex Plane Circle
demo_steps.narration: Looking straight down the time axis 'n' from the end of the helix, the entire 3D signal collapses into a 2D circle. As time progresses, the signal simply rotates counter-clockwise around this unit circle.

demo_steps.title: Damped Exponentials
demo_steps.narration: By decreasing the damping parameter, we multiply the helix by a decaying envelope. The cylinder collapses into an elegant tapering spiral, showing how Laplace and Z-transforms analyze decaying physical systems.

(2) This receding horizontal direction implies a camera azimuth in the negative range (approximately -55 degrees) so that both the positive R (Real) axis and the positive n (index) axis point to the right side of the viewport. (3) The vertical Imaginary axis remains perfectly vertical on screen, while the slight opening up of the horizontal R-n plane implies a moderate elevation angle of 25 degrees.

camera_view.view_notes: The vertical imaginary axis is perfectly aligned with the screen's vertical axis, while the Real and index axes form a wide-angle perspective extending to the right.

inline_constraints.explainers: Interactive hover states on the spheres reveal their coordinate triplets (n, Real, Imaginary).

inline_constraints.camera: Start in the specified orthographic view to perfectly overlay the original textbook page artwork.

demo_steps.title: The Complex Plane Circle
demo_steps.narration: Looking straight down the time axis 'n' from the end of the helix, the entire 3D signal collapses into a 2D circle. As time progresses, the signal simply rotates counter-clockwise around this unit circle.

demo_steps.title: Damped Exponentials
demo_steps.narration: By decreasing the damping parameter, we multiply the helix by a decaying envelope. The cylinder collapses into an elegant tapering spiral, showing how Laplace and Z-transforms analyze decaying physical systems.

interactionPlan.camera_suggestion: An orthographic viewpoint tilted slightly down and looking from the left quadrant to match the textbook's custom perspective, making all three axes clearly legible.
interactionPlan.view_reasoning: (1) The dominant time axis 'n' starts at the origin and runs diagonally towards the lower-right of the image space. (2) This receding horizontal direction implies a camera azimuth in the negative range (approximately -55 degrees) so that both the positive R (Real) axis and the positive n (index) axis point to the right side of the viewport. (3) The vertical Imaginary axis remains perfectly vertical on screen, while the slight opening up of the horizontal R-n plane implies a moderate elevation angle of 25 degrees.

camera_view.view_notes: The vertical imaginary axis is perfectly aligned with the screen's vertical axis, while the Real and index axes form a wide-angle perspective extending to the right.

inline_constraints.default_view: Must match the original wireframe axes layout, using black for the helix beads, red for the real projection, and green for the imaginary projection.
inline_constraints.visible_ui: A maximum of two thin, compact sliders for Frequency and Damping placed unobtrusively near the top or bottom edges.
inline_constraints.explainers: Interactive hover states on the spheres reveal their coordinate triplets (n, Real, Imaginary).
inline_constraints.framing: Maintain ample whitespace around the helical tail (near n=40) to match the original layout proportions.
inline_constraints.camera: Start in the specified orthographic view to perfectly overlay the original textbook page artwork.

interactionPlan.notes: Ensure the 'X' marks inside the black spheres are billboarded or rendered as crisp vector overlays so they remain legible from all camera angles. The connecting lines between the 3D helix and its projections should dynamically update when sliders are manipulated.

evaluation.geometry_accuracy_analysis: All key 3D elements—including the helical sample points, cross markers, projection curves (red and green), coordinate axes with arrowheads, and tick marks—are reconstructed as real 3D primitives. Their relative positions and spatial relationships are accurate. However, the default camera viewpoint is inverted/rotated compared to the reference; the n-axis points upwards and to the right in the render, whereas it points downwards and to the right in the original image.
evaluation.geometry_accuracy_improvement: Adjust the default camera azimuth and elevation angles so the n-axis points down-right, replicating the exact perspective of the original figure.
evaluation.interactivity_usability_analysis: The developer built three UI controls: a frequency slider (ω), a damping slider (σ), and an orbit controls toggle, all of which are fully functional and update the 3D helical geometry, its 2D projections, and textual value readouts in real-time. Additionally, a 5-step guided demo is integrated into the 3D scene using registerInteractive on the helix, red/green projection lines, and coordinate axes. Clicking these elements triggers smooth camera/parameter transitions corresponding to the planned pedagogical steps (e.g., collapsing the helix to look down the real or imaginary axis to reveal cosine/sine shapes).
evaluation.faithfulness_analysis: The rendered image captures the general composition, colors, and axis design. However, the trajectory of the 3D black spiral curve differs significantly; the original features a tight loop curling back on itself, whereas the rendered curve extends linearly along the n-axis.
discrepancies: The 3D black curve is much more extended along the n-axis instead of wrapping tightly as in the original.
Axis labels and numerical markers (like '20', '40') are positioned differently or missing.
evaluation.faithfulness_improvement: Adjust the mathematical parameterization of the spiral curve to increase the angular frequency or decay, forcing it to curl tightly back toward the center as shown in the reference.
evaluation.label_quality_analysis: The output contains most axis labels (I, R, n) and tick labels (1, -1), including the sub-caption '(a)'. However, the key sequence index labels '1' and '20' are missing along the curve, with only '40' partially visible.
evaluation.label_quality_improvement: Add clearly positioned, floating labels for sequence indices 1 and 20 near their corresponding curve positions.
evaluation.concept_accuracy_analysis: The generated figure illustrates the complex exponential wave z[n] = e^(j ω n) as a 3D helical signal where the axial direction is time (n), and the transverse axes are the Real (ℜ) and Imaginary (I) components. The real component projection (red cosine wave) is accurately mapped to the ℜ-n plane, and the imaginary component projection (green sine wave) is mapped to the I-n plane. The interactive demo steps successfully guide the user through aligning the camera down each axis to collapse the 3D helix into its 2D components (cosine, sine, and the complex unit circle) or applying damping to show decaying spirals. All labels, coordinates, and math relations are conceptually precise and correct.
evaluation.notes: While the interactive demo and conceptual design are excellent, the visualization suffers from an incorrect camera perspective and an overly stretched helix. The 3D spiral curve does not curl tightly like the reference, and critical labels for the sequence indices are misaligned or missing.
action_items: Adjust the 'mainView' azimuth and elevation parameters so that the n-axis projects downwards and to the right, replicating the source perspective.
Decrease 'nScale' and compress the spacing along the n-axis to make the helix and its 2D projections look tightly wound rather than linearly stretched.
Position the labels '1', '20', and '40' directly next to their corresponding points on the helix and projections.
Fine-tune the placement of the 'I', 'ℝ', and 'n' axis labels to align cleanly with the tips of their respective arrows.

feedback.rationale: The conceptual design is correct, but execution fixes are needed for camera perspective, compressing the helix scale along the n-axis, and improving label alignment.
